newsitem.title: ITALY: Cuban bishop say Castro could meet the Pope in Rome.
newsitem.headline: Cuban bishop say Castro could meet the Pope in Rome.

text.p: The Archbishop of Havana said on Tuesday that a meeting between Cuban President Fidel Castro and Pope John Paul in Rome next month was possible.
"If Castro comes to Rome for the World Food Summit I think he will see the Pope," Cardinal Jaime Ortega told Reuters after attending an international peace conference.
It is not yet known whether Castro will travel to Rome for the summit, organised by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) from November 13 to 17.

Asked about the possiblity of a trip by the Pope to Cuba, the only country in Latin America which he has not visited, Ortega said that it was "getting closer". He did not elaborate on a potential date.
Diplomatic sources in Rome have said previously that, if Castro did meet the Pope in November, he would probably invite him to Cuba, perhaps in 1997.
The Pope, recovering in a Rome hospital from an appendix operation, is scheduled to open the FAO World Food Summit.
Ortega confirmed the Vatican foreign minister, Jean-Louis Tauran, would visit Cuba from October 25 at the invitation of the government. He did not say whether he would meet Castro.
The meeting between the Pontiff and the Cuban leader would cap recent improvements in sometimes tense relations between the Roman Catholic Church and the government in Cuba.
Cuban authorities moved towards more relaxed relations with Christian churches in the early 1990s after years of tension following the 1959 revolution that brought Castro to power.
Membership in the Communist Party is no longer barred to the faithful and constitutional changes in 1992 outlawed religious discrimination in clearer terms.
Ties with the Roman Catholic Church have remained strained at times, notably over several calls in recent years by the island's Catholic bishops for political change.
